_comment: Guided exercises, batch 1. Adapted by the assistant from the titles and one-line purposes in the Strong for Yourself workbook index (Early Warning Sign Tracker, State Before / State After Tracker, Capacity Expansion Tracker). They are NOT extracts from the book and are drafts for Caroline to review and rewrite. Nothing a member enters is stored.

exercises.title: Early Warning Signs
exercises.subtitle: Noticing sooner
exercises.intro: Before a stress response builds, your system usually gives small signals. Noticing them sooner gives you more choice about what to do next. There are no right or wrong answers, and you can skip anything that doesn't fit. You can stop at any time.

steps.title: Early signs come first
steps.body: Think of a recent time you felt stretched or on edge. You don't need to relive it. Just keep it loosely in mind while you answer, and choose whatever feels true. If nothing fits, choose "Not sure yet".

steps.question: In your body, what do you usually notice first?

options.label: A tight jaw or clenched teeth

steps.question: Emotionally, what tends to show up early?
What tends to happen in your thinking?
What do you tend to do?

options.label: Say yes when I mean no
Tidy or try to control things

steps.question: How early do you usually notice these signs?
Which one early sign would be most helpful to watch for this week?
steps.help: A word or a few words is enough.
steps.placeholder: For example: my shoulders rising

summary.heading: Your early signs
summary.intro: This is your own list, in one place. Seeing it together can make the signs easier to spot.

closing.heading: Noticing is the first step
closing.message: Early signs are information, not a problem. You are not expected to catch every one. Even noticing one a little sooner gives you a little more choice.

exercises.title: State Before / State After
exercises.subtitle: What changes, and what doesn't
exercises.intro: A short check-in either side of a practice, so you can see how your own system responds. You are not aiming for a particular result, and nothing here is a test. You can stop at any time.

steps.title: Before you start
steps.body: Choose a practice you are about to do, or have just decided to do. It can be anything from a breath to a full guided practice. First, a quick check of how you are right now.

steps.question: Right now, how settled do you feel in your body?
Which word feels closest right now?

steps.title: Now do your practice
steps.body: Do the practice you chose, at your own pace. You can keep your eyes open, adapt it, or stop if it doesn't feel right. When you have finished, come back here.

steps.question: How settled do you feel in your body now?
Which word feels closest now?
Anything you noticed, however small?
steps.placeholder: For example: my breathing slowed

summary.heading: What you noticed
summary.intro: Here is your check-in, side by side.

closing.heading: Thank you for checking in
closing.message: Whether things shifted, stayed the same or felt different, you have learned something about how your system responds. That is useful, whichever way it went.

exercises.title: Capacity Expansion Tracker
exercises.subtitle: Where your resource is, right now
exercises.intro: Capacity is the resource you have available to hold what life is asking of you. This is a snapshot of where it is growing, steady, running low or draining away. It is not a score and there is no right answer. You can stop at any time.

steps.title: A snapshot, not a score
steps.body: We'll look at five areas of life. For each, choose what feels closest this week. "Draining away" means resource that leaks out without you choosing it, such as hours lost to worry or energy spent on things you didn't mean to take on.

steps.question: Physical: your sleep, energy and body
Emotional: how much you can feel and hold
Mental: your focus and decision-making
Relational: connection and support
Practical: your time, money and day-to-day load
Which area feels most worth protecting this week?
What is one small thing that could protect it?
steps.placeholder: For example: a firm stop time in the evening

summary.heading: Your capacity snapshot
summary.intro: This is where things stand this week. It will change with sleep, load, support and season.

closing.heading: A snapshot, not a verdict
closing.message: Seeing where your resource is running low is how you decide where to protect it. You don't have to fix everything at once. One small, realistic step is plenty.

exercises.title: Future Self Capacity Map
exercises.subtitle: What would help it become possible
exercises.intro: Think of something you would like to become possible for you, without turning it into pressure. This exercise connects it to the resources that would support it, so you can see what is already there and what is not yet. There are no right answers, and you can stop at any time.

steps.title: Start small and real
steps.body: Choose one thing you would like to be possible in the next year. It might be a change at work, a different pace of life, a creative project or a closer relationship. Keep it modest. It only needs to matter to you.

steps.question: In a few words, what would you like to become possible?
steps.placeholder: For example: a calmer start to my mornings

steps.question: Which of these would it need most?
Which of those do you already have in place?
steps.help: Choose any that feel at least partly true.

steps.question: How steady does it feel to move toward this right now?
steps.help: This is information, not a grade.

steps.question: What is one small, supported step that could build what is missing?
steps.placeholder: For example: asking a friend to check in weekly

summary.heading: Your map
summary.intro: This is what you would like, what it would need, and what you already have.

closing.heading: A map, not a plan
closing.message: You do not have to build everything at once. Seeing what is already in place, and what is not yet, shows you where one small step could help most.

exercises.title: Receiving and Support Map
exercises.subtitle: Who and what holds you up
exercises.intro: Support is easier to use when you can see it. This exercise maps what supports you now, what kind of support it is, and what makes it hard to receive. There are no right answers, and you can stop at any time.

steps.title: Looking at support
steps.body: Think about the past few weeks. Notice who or what helped you stay on your feet, even in small ways. Choose whatever feels true.

steps.question: Who or what supports you right now?

options.label: Faith or a sense of meaning

steps.question: What kind of support is it?
How easy is it for you to receive support?
What most gets in the way of receiving it?

options.label: I do not want to be a burden
I am used to managing alone
I do not know what to ask for
I am not sure it will help
Nothing much gets in the way

steps.question: What is one small way you could let in a little more support this week?
steps.placeholder: For example: telling one person how the week is going

summary.heading: Your support map
summary.intro: Here is what holds you up, and what makes it harder to lean on.

closing.heading: Support is a skill, too
closing.message: Receiving is something you can practise in small steps. Noticing what already holds you up is a good place to begin.

exercises.title: Nervous System Scorecard
exercises.subtitle: A snapshot across the five conditions
exercises.intro: This is a snapshot of how available five things feel to you right now: safety, capacity, availability, expansion and participation. It is not a grade and there is no good or bad result. It simply shows where you might want more support. You can stop at any time.

steps.title: A snapshot, not a grade
steps.body: Answer for roughly this past week. Go with your first sense. If a question does not fit, choose the number that feels closest.

steps.question: Safety: how easy is it to feel safe enough to settle?
Capacity: how easy is it to hold what life is asking of you?
Availability: how easy is it to reach your own feelings, needs and other people?
Expansion: how easy is it to move beyond what is familiar, at your own pace?
Participation: how easy is it to take part in the parts of life that matter to you?
Which one would you most like more support with right now?
Anything you would like to remember about this snapshot?

summary.heading: Your snapshot
summary.intro: This is how things feel this week. It will change.

closing.heading: Where support could go
closing.message: A lower number is not a failure. It points to where a little support or a small step could help. You can come back to this any time to see what has changed.

exercises.title: The Smallest Meaningful Movement
exercises.subtitle: One manageable step toward your life
exercises.intro: This exercise helps you choose one small, realistic step toward something that matters to you. Participation is not about doing more or being productive. It is about taking part in your own life, one ordinary moment at a time. You can stop at any time.

steps.question: Which area of life would you like to take part in a little more?
What is one small thing you could do in the next day or two?
steps.help: Smaller than you think. A few minutes is plenty.
steps.placeholder: For example: ten minutes with a friend, no phone

steps.question: What would make it easier?

options.label: Nothing, I can do it as it is

steps.question: How doable does it feel?
steps.help: If it feels like a stretch, choose a smaller step.

steps.question: When could you do it?

summary.heading: Your step
summary.intro: Here is the step you chose.

closing.heading: Small is enough
closing.message: One ordinary moment of taking part counts. If the step turns out to be too big, make it smaller. There is no wrong way to begin.

exercises.title: Pause Before Responding
exercises.subtitle: A moment before the automatic reply
exercises.intro: Sometimes a message, a request or a conversation pulls an automatic reaction out of us before we have chosen anything. This exercise gives you a short pause first. You do not have to respond in any particular way, and you can stop at any time.

steps.question: What are you about to respond to?

options.label: A message I need to answer
A request I feel I should agree to
Something I feel I should apologise for

steps.question: What is the pull right now?

steps.title: Take a short pause
steps.body: Let your feet rest on the floor and notice what is supporting you. Breathe out a little more slowly than you breathe in, only if that feels comfortable. Notice your jaw and shoulders, and let them soften if they will. There is no hurry.

steps.question: How much room do you feel you have now?
What would you like to do next?

closing.heading: The pause is yours
closing.message: You can take a moment before responding, whatever the situation asks. Even a few seconds can give you a little more choice.

exercises.title: Delegation Tracker
exercises.subtitle: Sharing the load
exercises.intro: Carrying everything yourself uses up capacity. This exercise helps you notice what you hold, what you could share, and how it feels to let others help. There are no right answers, and you can stop at any time.

steps.title: What are you carrying?
steps.body: Think about the past week. Notice the tasks and responsibilities that landed on you, big or small, and choose whatever feels true.

steps.question: Where are you carrying most?
Which one thing could someone else share or take on?
steps.placeholder: For example: the weekly food shop

steps.question: Who could help, or what could make it lighter?
How easy would it be for you to ask or hand it over?
steps.help: If it feels hard, that is useful to notice.

steps.question: What makes handing things over hard?

options.label: It is quicker if I do it
They will not do it my way
I do not want to burden anyone
I feel I should manage it myself

steps.question: What is one small way to try it this week?
steps.placeholder: For example: asking for help with one task

summary.heading: Your load
summary.intro: Here is what you are carrying and one way to share it.

closing.heading: You do not have to carry it all
closing.message: Sharing a little of the load protects the resource you need for what matters. Start with one small thing, and let it be imperfect.

exercises.title: Trigger Map
exercises.subtitle: What sets you off, gently
exercises.intro: Some situations set off a strong reaction faster than we expect. This exercise helps you notice one of them from a steady distance. Choose something mild, not the hardest thing in your life. You can stop at any time, and nothing you enter is saved.

steps.title: Choose something mild
steps.body: Pick a situation that stirs a small to medium reaction, not the most painful thing. If thinking about it feels like too much, stop here and choose something smaller, or leave the exercise.

steps.question: Where does it tend to happen?
What tends to set it off?
What do you notice in your body first?
What do you usually do next?
How strong is this reaction, usually?
steps.help: If it is high, choose a gentler situation next time.

steps.question: What is one early sign you could watch for next time?
steps.placeholder: For example: my shoulders rising

summary.heading: Your map
summary.intro: This is a picture of one pattern, from a steady distance.

closing.heading: Seeing it is enough for today
closing.message: A reaction that makes sense is not a flaw. Noticing what sets it off, and where you feel it first, gives you a little more room next time.

exercises.title: Evening Regulation Reflection
exercises.subtitle: Closing the day gently
exercises.intro: A short reflection to close the day: what asked the most of you, what helped, and what you would like to set down. It is not a review or a grade. You can stop at any time.

steps.question: How did today feel overall for your system?
What asked the most of you today?
What helped, even a little?
What would you like to set down before sleep?
steps.placeholder: For example: the unanswered email

steps.question: What is one kind thing you can say to yourself about today?
steps.placeholder: For example: I did what I could with what I had

summary.heading: Today, in brief
summary.intro: Here is how the day looked.

closing.heading: The day is done
closing.message: You can set down what is left until tomorrow. Rest is part of how your system recovers, and it does not have to be earned.

exercises.title: Looking Back, Looking Forward
exercises.subtitle: What you have carried, and where you are heading
exercises.intro: This exercise looks briefly backward to what has been true for you, and then forward to a direction that feels like yours. It is not about fixing the past or planning everything ahead. You can stop at any time.

steps.title: Two quiet glances
steps.body: First you will look back over a period of your life, gently. Then you will look toward a direction. Keep both modest. Choose what feels true, and leave out anything that feels too heavy.

steps.question: Which stretch of time are you looking back over?

options.label: A bigger chapter of my life

steps.question: What have you carried or lived through in that time?
What is something you got through, or did well, even if it was small?
steps.placeholder: For example: I kept going when it was hard

steps.question: What direction would you like to lean toward?

options.label: I am not sure yet, and that is okay

steps.question: What is one small step that leans that way?
steps.placeholder: For example: a short walk three times this week

steps.question: How ready does that step feel?
steps.help: Not ready is a valid answer.

summary.heading: Back and forward
summary.intro: Here is where you have been and the direction you chose.

closing.heading: One step at a time
closing.message: Looking back shows what you have already carried. Looking forward does not have to be big. One small step in a direction that feels like yours is plenty.

exercises.title: Support Plan
exercises.subtitle: Who to turn to, and how to ask
exercises.intro: A support plan is a short list you can reach for when things are hard, so you do not have to work it out in the moment. You choose who or what helps, and how you would ask. You can stop at any time, and nothing you enter is saved.

steps.title: Before you need it
steps.body: Think of a time recently when things felt like too much. What would you have liked to have in place? Choose whatever feels true.

steps.question: When would you most like support?

options.label: When I feel lonely or cut off
When I have a hard decision
When my body feels worn out
Late at night or early morning

steps.question: Who or what could you turn to?
What could you say to ask for support?
steps.help: A line you could copy and paste is fine.
steps.placeholder: For example: I am having a hard day. Could I talk for ten minutes?

steps.question: What kind of help would you want most?
How willing do you feel to use this plan?
steps.help: Not very is information, not failure.

steps.question: What is one thing you could do this week to put it in place?
steps.placeholder: For example: telling one person they are on my list

summary.heading: Your support plan
summary.intro: Here is the plan you can reach for.

closing.heading: Ready when you are
closing.message: Having a plan means you do not have to decide everything when you are low on resource. If you ever feel unsafe or in crisis, please contact a professional or emergency service.

exercises.title: Participation Goals
exercises.subtitle: What taking part means to you
exercises.intro: Participation is not about doing more or being productive. It is about taking part in the parts of your life that matter to you. This exercise helps you name what that means for you right now, in your own terms. There are no right answers, and you can stop at any time.

steps.title: In your own terms
steps.body: Think about the past few weeks. Notice where you felt most like a participant in your own life, and where you felt on the edge of it. Choose whatever feels true.

steps.question: Where would you like to take part a little more?
Which matters most to you this season?
What would taking part look like there, in your own words?
steps.placeholder: For example: sharing a meal without checking my phone

steps.question: How much does this feel like yours, rather than something you should do?
steps.help: If it feels like a should, that is worth noticing.

steps.question: How much capacity do you have for it right now?
What is one thing that would make it a little more possible?
steps.placeholder: For example: clearing one evening a week

summary.heading: Your goals
summary.intro: Here is what taking part means to you right now.

closing.heading: Yours to define
closing.message: What counts as taking part is yours to decide, and it can change with the season you are in. You do not have to do it all at once.

exercises.title: Participation Bridge Tracker
exercises.subtitle: From noticing to one small action
exercises.intro: Reflection helps most when it connects to daily life. This exercise takes something you have noticed and builds a small bridge to one real action. There are no right answers, and you can stop at any time.

steps.title: Carrying it across
steps.body: Bring to mind something from a recent practice, exercise or moment that stayed with you. It does not need to be big.

steps.question: What are you bringing across?

options.label: Something I noticed in a practice
Something I would like more of

steps.question: In a few words, what is it?
steps.placeholder: For example: I feel better after a walk

steps.question: Where in daily life could it show up?
What is one small action that would carry it across?
steps.help: Small enough to do without much planning.
steps.placeholder: For example: a ten-minute walk after lunch

steps.question: How doable does it feel?
steps.help: If it feels like a stretch, make it smaller.

steps.question: When could you do it?
What might get in the way, and what could help?

summary.heading: Your bridge
summary.intro: Here is what you noticed and the small action that carries it across.

closing.heading: A small bridge is enough
closing.message: Connecting what you notice to one ordinary action is how reflection becomes part of your life. If the step is too big, make it smaller.

exercises.title: Capacity Protection Plan
exercises.subtitle: Protecting what taking part needs
exercises.intro: Taking part in your life takes resource. This exercise helps you notice what drains yours, what protects it, and one limit you could try. It is a plan for protecting your capacity, not a list of things you must do. There are no right answers, and you can stop at any time.

steps.title: Protecting your resource
steps.body: Think about the weeks when you have had enough left for the things that matter, and the weeks when you have not. Notice what tends to make the difference.

steps.question: What most drains the resource you need to take part?
What most helps protect it?
What is one limit or boundary you would like to try?
steps.placeholder: For example: no work messages after 8pm

steps.question: How hard would it be to keep?
steps.help: If it feels very hard, choose a smaller limit.

steps.question: What could make it easier to keep?
Who could you tell, so it is easier to keep?

options.label: Just myself. I will write it down

summary.heading: Your plan
summary.intro: Here is how you could protect your capacity.

closing.heading: Protection makes room
closing.message: Protecting your capacity is what makes taking part possible. Start with one small limit, and let it change as your life does.

practices.title: Early Warning Signs
practices.description: A short guided exercise to notice your own early signs of stress, in your body, feelings, thinking and behaviour. You choose what fits, see it back in one place, and decide one sign to watch for.

practices.title: State Before / State After
practices.description: A quick check-in either side of any practice, so you can see how your own system responds. Rate how settled you feel before and after, and notice what changes, or doesn't.

practices.title: Capacity Expansion Tracker
practices.description: A snapshot of your resource across five areas of life: physical, emotional, mental, relational and practical. See where it is growing, steady, running low or draining away, and choose one area to protect.

practices.title: Future Self Capacity Map
practices.description: Connect something you would like to become possible with the resources that would support it. See what is already in place and what is not yet, and choose one small step.

practices.title: Receiving and Support Map
practices.description: Map who and what supports you now, what kind of support it is, and what makes it hard to receive, then choose one small way to let in a little more.

practices.title: Nervous System Scorecard
practices.description: A snapshot of how available safety, capacity, availability, expansion and participation feel right now. Not a grade: it shows where a little support could help.

practices.title: The Smallest Meaningful Movement
practices.description: Choose one small, realistic step toward something that matters to you. Participation is about taking part in your life, not doing more.

practices.title: Pause Before Responding
practices.description: A short pause before an automatic reply. Notice what is pulling at you, take a moment, then choose what to do next.

practices.title: Delegation Tracker
practices.description: Notice what you are carrying, choose one thing that could be shared, and see what makes handing things over hard.

practices.title: Trigger Map
practices.description: Look at one mild trigger from a steady distance: where it happens, what sets it off, what you notice in your body first, and one early sign to watch for.

practices.title: Evening Regulation Reflection
practices.description: A short end-of-day reflection: what asked the most of you, what helped, what to set down, and one kind thing to say to yourself.

practices.title: Looking Back, Looking Forward
practices.description: Look gently back at what you have carried, then forward to a direction that feels like yours, and choose one small step.

practices.title: Support Plan
practices.description: A short plan you can reach for when things are hard: when you would want support, who or what could help, and how you would ask.

practices.title: Participation Goals
practices.description: Name what taking part in your life means to you right now: the areas that matter, what it would look like, and what would make it a little more possible.

practices.title: Participation Bridge Tracker
practices.description: Take something you have noticed and build a small bridge to one real action in daily life: what it is, where it fits, when, and what might get in the way.

practices.title: Capacity Protection Plan
practices.description: Notice what drains the resource you need to take part, what protects it, and one limit you could try, with what would make it easier to keep.
